title: [Repost with dev details] How I built a 3-renderer pixel art ARPG with AI coding agents, and where the AI failed hard
author: AKCeifador
selftext:
My last post got removed for not explaining the process (fair, rule 4). So here's the actual dev breakdown, plus answers to the questions in the comments.



\*\*What the game is (core loop)\*\*

The Old Circle is a story-driven action RPG dungeon crawler (closer to Diablo than to Vampire Survivors). You pick 1 of 5 classes, go down hand-built dungeon floors across 7 chapters, fight 21 bosses with multi-phase mechanics, and come back to a village hub to forge gear, socket glyphs and runes, and spend skill points. PC + controller, online co-op through Steam.



\*\*Tools\*\*

\- Code: plain JavaScript (HTML5 canvas + Three.js), a Node server with a shared simulation (the server is authoritative, and the client only renders), and Electron + steamworks.js for the PC build.

\- AI: almost all the code was written with an AI coding agent (Claude Code) running in my repo. I direct, review, play and reject; the agent writes, tests and fixes.



\*\*How the AI workflow actually works\*\*

1. \*\*Parallel agents in separate git worktrees.\*\* For big jobs I split the work by chapter or biome and run several agents at once, each in its own worktree and branch. Then an "orchestrator" agent merges the branches after running the test suite. The isometric renderer was built this way: around 7 agents, one per chapter, plus engine and props agents.

2. \*\*Everything is checked by scripts, not by vibes.\*\* The agents write their own test tools: simulation tests per chapter, a test that fires every skill, save round-trip tests, a controller test, and an i18n checker for 7 languages.

3. \*\*Automated screenshots.\*\* Headless Chrome is driven over CDP, with a virtual clock injected into the game, so every frame is deterministic. The agents take screenshots of every boss phase or skill and actually \*look\* at them before saying "done".

4. \*\*Pixel art linters.\*\* For the isometric bosses, an agent wrote a checker that flags orphan pixels, checkerboard dithering noise, holes and doubles in outlines, shadows that don't sit under the feet, scale mismatch against the classic sprites, and pieces clipping through each other. Orphan pixels went from up to 1,700 per boss to zero.

5. \*\*Bot playtesting.\*\* Last night I had 2 bot agents play the whole game end to end, one in the Classic view and one in Isometric, switching class every chapter and pressing real keys. A third agent fixed bugs live as they were reported. That gave about 30 fixes in one night. Some real ones:

   \- a boss puzzle impossible because it triggered during the boss's immune phase;

   \- puzzle numbers hidden under the guide arrow;

   \- the irreversible ending choice happening with zero confirmation;

   \- a boss flashing white 100% of the time under damage-over-time effects.

6. \*\*Balance sims.\*\* Headless combat simulations (DPS per class per chapter, boss fight duration in 4 difficulties, XP pacing, loot economy) produce a report. I decide the changes.



\*\*The 3 visual modes (the trailer's main point)\*\*

The same game state is drawn by 3 renderers you can switch at runtime:

\- \*\*Classic:\*\* top-down canvas pixel art.

\- \*\*HD-2D:\*\* Three.js with pixel sprites on 3D planes, real lights and shadows.

\- \*\*Isometric:\*\* a full separate engine. Heroes come from a small 3D rig projected to pixel art in 8 directions (90 skins). It has 21 biomes with their own props, plus isometric versions of 150 monsters and 21 bosses.



\*\*Where AI failed (honestly)\*\*

\- \*\*Character art.\*\* I asked for a redesign of my first boss. The AI produced two concepts from a 3D rig: horrible. Then two more as hand-placed pixel grids: still horrible. I kept the original. AI is great at systems, tooling and consistency, but it still can't match a good human-made sprite.

\- \*\*Hardware.\*\* 8 headless Chromes in parallel reset my GPU driver. Now there's a shared queue (max 2–3 browsers) and a CPU watchdog that throttles the agents.

\- \*\*"Done" is not done.\*\* Without screenshot checks and tests, agents happily report fixed bugs that aren't fixed.



\*\*How the trailer was made (someone asked)\*\*

\- \*\*Footage:\*\* 100% real gameplay recorded frame by frame through the virtual clock, with scripted bots and a cinematic camera.

\- \*\*Graphics:\*\* motion graphics drawn in canvas.

\- \*\*Audio:\*\* music and sound effects synthesized in code (OfflineAudioContext). The voices are Windows' built-in text-to-speech, robotic on purpose for the joke.

\- \*\*Edit:\*\* assembled with ffmpeg. There are PT-BR and EN versions, horizontal and vertical.



\*\*Mobile?\*\* I tried, and dropped it to focus on PC + controller.



Happy to answer anything about the agent setup, the isometric pipeline or the bot playtests.



Wishlist: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5596460/The\_Old\_Circle\_Ecos\_da\_Masmorra/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5596460/The_Old_Circle_Ecos_da_Masmorra/)

comments.author: CipherAndChloride
comments.body: interesting approach with parallel agents but i always worry about merge conflicts when orchestrating multiple writers in blockchains or codebases. did you have to write custom diff logic for the orchestrator agent?

replies.author: AKCeifador
replies.body: Nope, plain git merge. Each agent works in its own worktree and branch, owns a fixed set of files (one per chapter, for example), and can't touch the shared engine. Engine changes are written down as requests and done later by a single agent. The orchestrator merges one branch at a time and runs the tests between merges. Conflicts basically disappeared once ownership was clear.

Hands down the best comment, hahaha!

You’re spot on. I have over 15 years of experience, though it’s in software development. I started my career in game development and later shifted to software, but now I’m trying to combine both—and with AI, it’s been absolutely magnificent!

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body: The pixel-art linter is a smart idea — orphan pixels, broken outlines and shadows that don't sit under the feet are exactly what makes generated sprites feel unfinished. Two checks I'd add for the 8-direction isometric heroes: palette flicker (a midtone that appears on one facing and not the others) and whether the back view is still the same character. Coats and hair often morph from behind even when the front looks fine. Linters catch the mechanical errors, but silhouette identity and a consistent outline width are still easier to judge at 1x by eye.
